Project 3: Linear Regression¶

In this project, you'll work with a large data set from Cook County, Illinois (the county where Chicago is located). This data set contains over 500,000 records with 62 features, including Sale Price. Our ultimate goal will be to predict Sale Price from some combination of the other 61 features. Along the way, you will:

  • Work with a large data set, including addressing issues in real-world data
  • Review EDA methods, including cleaning data and adding columns
  • Practice linear regression, feature engineering, and model selection

This project will have two phases. You will start with scaffolded questions, and ultimately fit and evaluate your own model.

Warning: The questions for these phases increase in difficulty as the assignment goes on.

  • On phase 1 (questions 1-9), questions 7-9 all have multiple parts. You also should aim to be through question 11 by the phase 1 deadline, but only need to be through question 9.
  • On phase 2, there are only 6 questions -- but the last two are the bulk of the second phase. In particular, in the last 2 questions, you will do all of: exploratory work to motivate a strong model; testing and evaluating at least five models; picking a final model that best fits the data; and building a full data science pipeline to implement that model and all the necessary feature engineering. Start early.

Partner Information¶

You are allowed to work with a partner on this project. If you do, only one of you should submit each phase, but that person should add their partner to the submission.

Credits¶

This project is adapted from Project A in the Data 100 course, with permission of the Data 100 teaching team. Please do not post or share your solutions.

Phase 1: Due Wednesday 3/25 at 10pm¶

In phase 1, you'll explore the data, perform some EDA methods, and fit simple linear regression models.

Getting Acquainted with the Data¶

Again, this data set has 62 features. An explanation of each variable can be found in the included codebook.txt file in the project directory. Some of the rows and columns in the codebook have been filtered out to ensure this assignment doesn't become overly long when dealing with data cleaning and formatting.

The data are split into training and test sets. You have access to a training set with 163,834 observations. There is a separate test set with 33,796 observations that you do not have access to, but that you will eventually (in phase 2) use to benchmark your model.

Let's first extract the data from the cook_county_data.zip. Run the cells below to load the data and then verify that it is as described:

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Later, you will be building a linear regression model that predicts sales prices. First, it's important to understand how the structure of the data informs such a model. In this section, we will make a series of exploratory visualizations and do some feature engineering in preparation for your final prediction task.

Question 6 Based on the above analysis, we should pick a cutoff to get rid of smaller, probably unrepresentative Sale Prices. The sales price also has strong right skew, and so we will likely find it helpful to apply a log transformation (e.g. attempting to predict log(Sale Price) instead of Sale Price in our future regression models). Create a dataframe training_data that is identifical to initial_data except with the following changes:

  1. Filter the data to only include homes that were at least \$500 (inclusive) and at most \$50,000,000 (inclusive). This will remove the absurdly expensive house we previously identified as erroneous as well as the small values that likely don't correspond to real home values.

  2. Add a new Log Sale Price column that contains the log of the sale prices. Use np.log which calculates the natural log (i.e. log base $e$ / $\ln$)

The slope means that each additional square foot is associated with an average increase of about 0.000666 in Log Sale Price, so an extra 100 square feet corresponds to about 0.0666 more in log price. The relationship is positive, but the fit is only moderate, with R^2 = 0.322, visible curvature in the scatterplot, some non-constant spread in the residuals, and tail departures in the QQ plot.

Question 7c: Based on the above, which do you think will be a better predictor of Log Sale Price? Explain your reasoning, drawing off of the above work.

Log Building Square Feet is the better predictor because it makes the relationship more linear, slightly improves the fit (R^2 rises from about 0.322 to about 0.348), and gives cleaner residual patterns.

Question 8a Write a function split_desc that will take in a description (like the above, as a string) and use string split methods to return a list of the form [number rooms, number bedrooms, number bathrooms]. Each should be a float. Hint: the string split method will help! You do not need to edit any markdown cells for this question.

In [181]:
# BEGIN QUESTION 8a
def split_desc(description):
    details = description.split("It has a total of ")[1]
    pieces = details.split(", ")
    
    rooms = float(pieces[0].split()[0])
    bedrms = float(pieces[1].split()[0])
    baths = float(pieces[2].split()[1])
    
    return [rooms, bedrms, baths]
# END QUESTION 8a

        print("Public test for 8a passed")
    else:

except:

# BEGIN QUESTION 10a

def find_expensive_neighborhoods(df, n=3):
    neighborhoods = (df.groupby("Neighborhood Code")["Sale Price"]
                     .median()
                     .nlargest(n)
                     .index)
    
    return [int(code) for code in neighborhoods]

Question 12c How do the $R^2$ compare for your model? How do you interpret the coefficient of num_bedrm and how do you explain the fact that it's negative and statistically significant? How do you interpret the coefficient of Wall Material Cat_Stucco?

mod2 has a lower R² and lower training MSE than mod1 because adding more predictors always allows OLS to fit the training data at least as well. The num_bedrm coefficient is negative: after controlling for building square footage, more bedrooms means each room is smaller on average, which signals lower quality or a more cramped layout—hence lower sale prices. The Wall Material Cat_Stucco coefficient represents the difference in log sale price between stucco-walled homes and masonry-walled homes (the dropped reference category), holding all other predictors constant. A positive coefficient would mean stucco homes sell for a higher price than masonry homes of the same size and bedroom count.

Building a Pipeline¶

Your main task of this stage of the project will be to come up with a model that is as predictive as possible. Ultimately, you will be (1) fitting/training your model on data you have access to (the data in training_data) and (2) testing it on data you do not have access to (which will evaluate if your model is actually representatitive of reality or if it is overfit to training data).

To get to that point, lets formalize some of our EDA into a data science pipeline (and yes, we'll be using our old friends .pipe and .assign). First, lets split your data into a local training and test set. This will allow you to train your models on your local training set, and test them on your local test set, to help you avoid overfitting.

In [203]:
train_split, test_split = train_test_split(training_data, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
print("Local Training Data Size: ", train_split.shape[0])
print("Local Test Data Size: ", test_split.shape[0])

Local Training Data Size:  108099
Local Test Data Size:  27025

Carefully review the next two code cells. The first builds a starter pipeline based on our EDA

  • log_transform will create our Log Sale Price and Log Building Square Feet columns
  • add_intercept adds an intercept column to a data frame
  • select_vars will be used to select just the explanatory features we want to fit our model on
  • filter_training_data will be used to filter out any observations that may skew our training data
  • train_and_predict puts these pieces together into a pipeline that we can run directly on loaded data.
  • It uses filter_training_data to...filter the training data
  • It pipes in log_transform and add_intercept to add features we've seen may be useful
  • It trains a model based on training data and uses that model to predict test data. Note that the model only trains using features in varlist

The next code cell runs the pipeline "from start to finish"

  • It loads in data directly from the CSV
  • It gets the same test/train splits as above
  • It filters down the training data using filter_training_data
  • It uses train_and_predict to get predictions on both the test and train set, and then prints out the MSE on both

Make sure you understand the code below, then run both cells to see how they work and see the MSE of one of the first models you explored in phase 1!

In [204]:
# DO NOT CHANGE THIS CELL
def log_transforms(df):
    """ 
    Input a DataFrame df with columns Sale Price and Building Square Feet
    Returns a new DataFrame that adds the log of each of these
    """
    # Note: This is slightly different formatting for assign than we've seen before
    # It works the exact same, but encasing it in a dictionary allows
    # us to create variable names with spaces in them
    return df.assign(**{
        "Log Sale Price": np.log(df["Sale Price"]),
        "Log Building Square Feet": np.log(df["Building Square Feet"])
    })

def add_intercept(df):
    """
    Input a DataFrame df.  
    Returns a new DataFrame with an intercept column
    """
    return df.assign(intercept = 1)


def select_vars(df, varlist):
    """
    Filters down DataFrame df to just the columns in varlist,
    which will be used for prediction
    """
    return df[varlist]

def filter_training_data(df):
    """
    Filters the training data. 
    You may add additional conditions here to remove outliers from your training set.
    Note: these filters will not be applied to the test set.  Only use this filter
    function if you want to remove outliers from your train set for better model fitting
    """
    # Start with the baseline filter from Phase 1
    filtered_df = df[(df['Sale Price'] >= 500) & (df['Sale Price'] <= 50000000)].copy()
    
    return filtered_df


def train_and_predict(train_df, test_df):
    """The full pipeline!  Takes in a training set and a test set.
    Applies any feature engineering to your training set and test set
    Trains a model on your updated train_df, using just a selection
    of columns in varlist.  Then evaluates that model on a test set,
    returning predictions for that test set."""
    # Filter Training Data
    train_filtered = filter_training_data(train_df)
    
    # Feature Engineering 
    train_df = train_filtered.pipe(log_transforms).pipe(add_intercept)
    test_df = test_df.pipe(log_transforms).pipe(add_intercept)
    
    # Select the variables you would like to use in your model
    varlist = ["intercept", "Log Building Square Feet"]
    

    # Fit the model on the training data and get predictions for the test set
    X_train = select_vars(train_df, varlist)
    X_test = select_vars(test_df, varlist)
    y_train = train_df["Log Sale Price"]    
    model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train).fit()
    predictions = model.predict(X_test)
    
    return predictions

def log_transforms(df):
    """
    Input a DataFrame df with columns Sale Price and Building Square Feet
    Returns a new DataFrame that adds the log of each of these
    """
    return df.assign(**{
        "Log Sale Price": np.log(df["Sale Price"]),
        "Log Building Square Feet": np.log(df["Building Square Feet"])
    })

def add_intercept(df):
    """
    Input a DataFrame df.
    Returns a new DataFrame with an intercept column
    """
    return df.assign(intercept = 1)


def select_vars(df, varlist):
    """

    which will be used for prediction
    """

# You can edit this one if you'd like to change how you filter data
def filter_training_data(df):
    """
    Filters the training data.
    You may add additional conditions here to remove outliers from your training set.
    Note: these filters will not be applied to the test set.  Only use this filter
    function if you want to remove outliers from your train set for better model fitting

# BEGIN QUESTION 13a

def add_bedrm(df):
    """Adds num_bedrm column by parsing the Description text."""
    def get_bedrm(description):
        details = description.split("It has a total of ")[1]
        pieces = details.split(", ")
        return float(pieces[1].split()[0])
    return df.assign(num_bedrm=df["Description"].apply(get_bedrm))

def id_expensive(df):
    """Adds in_expensive column: 1.0 if house is in top 10 most expensive
    neighborhoods by median sale price, 0.0 otherwise."""
    median_by_nbhd = df.groupby("Neighborhood Code")["Sale Price"].median()
    top10_nbhds = list(median_by_nbhd.nlargest(10).index)
    return df.assign(in_expensive=np.where(
        df["Neighborhood Code"].isin(top10_nbhds), 1.0, 0.0
    ))

def expand_wall_material(df):
    """Creates Wall Material Cat column and 3 dummy columns (drop_first=True drops Masonry)."""
    wall_map = {1: "Wood", 2: "Masonry", 3: "Wood&Masonry", 4: "Stucco"}
    df = df.assign(**{"Wall Material Cat": df["Wall Material"].map(wall_map)})
    # Manually create the three dummies to ensure consistent columns on train and test
    for cat in ["Stucco", "Wood", "Wood&Masonry"]:
        col = f"Wall Material Cat_{cat}"
        df = df.assign(**{col: (df["Wall Material Cat"] == cat).astype(int)})
    return df

# END QUESTION 13a

def train_and_predict(train_df, test_df):
    """The full pipeline!  Takes in a training set and a test set.
    Applies any feature engineering to your training set and test set
    Trains a model on your updated train_df, using just a selection
    of columns in varlist.  Then evaluates that model on a test set,
    returning predictions for that test set."""
    train_filtered = filter_training_data(train_df)

    train_df = (train_filtered.pipe(log_transforms)
                .pipe(add_intercept)
                .pipe(add_bedrm)
                .pipe(id_expensive)
                .pipe(expand_wall_material))
    test_df =  (test_df.pipe(log_transforms)
                .pipe(add_intercept)
                .pipe(add_bedrm)
                .pipe(id_expensive)
                .pipe(expand_wall_material))

    varlist = ["intercept", "Log Building Square Feet", "num_bedrm",
                 "in_expensive", "Wall Material Cat_Stucco",
                 "Wall Material Cat_Wood", "Wall Material Cat_Wood&Masonry"]

    X_train = select_vars(train_df, varlist)
    X_test = select_vars(test_df, varlist)
    y_train = train_df["Log Sale Price"]
    model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train).fit()
    predictions = model.predict(X_test)

    return predictions

Question 13b: Briefly explain why you know the train MSE should be less than 0.6529622297647072 (i.e. in the initial pipeline I provided you that just did a simple linear regression using Log Building Square Feet). Why is the train MSE not exactly the same as what you found after question 12c for mod2?

The training MSE in Q13a must be less than 0.6529622297647072 because OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals on the training set. Adding more predictors (num_bedrm, in_expensive, and the wall-material dummies) can only decrease or maintain the in-sample SSR, so the training MSE is always <= that of a simpler model.

The training MSE here differs from mod2.mse_resid because: (1) Different training data: Q13a's pipeline is fit on an 80% train split of training_data, while mod2 was fit on all of training_data. (2) Different price filter: filter_training_data caps Sale Price at $5M, while training_data includes homes up to $50M. Different observations yield different coefficient estimates and a different MSE.

# Question 15
# Use this cell to create your final pipeline.  Change/add ONLY where indicated.

# Do NOT change the first three functions:
def log_transforms(df):
    """
    Input a DataFrame df with columns Sale Price and Building Square Feet
    Returns a new DataFrame that adds the log of each of these
    """
    return df.assign(**{
        "Log Sale Price": np.log(df["Sale Price"]),
        "Log Building Square Feet": np.log(df["Building Square Feet"])
    })

def add_intercept(df):
    """
    Input a DataFrame df.
    Returns a new DataFrame with an intercept column
    """
    return df.assign(intercept = 1)


def select_vars(df, varlist):
    """
    Filters down DataFrame df to just the columns in varlist,
    which will be used for prediction
    """
    return df[varlist]

# You can edit this one if you'd like to change how you filter data
def filter_training_data(df):
    """
    Filters the training data.
    Removes implausible sale prices, outlier building sizes, and
    non-arms-length transactions (Pure Market Filter == 0).
    """
    filtered_df = df[
        (df['Sale Price'] >= 500) &
        (df['Sale Price'] <= 50000000) &
        (df['Building Square Feet'] >= 200) &
        (df['Building Square Feet'] <= 15000) &
        (df['Pure Market Filter'] == 1)
    ].copy()
    return filtered_df


# Helper functions

def add_bedrm(df):
    """Adds num_bedrm column by parsing the Description text."""
    def get_bedrm(desc):
        details = desc.split("It has a total of ")[1]
        pieces = details.split(", ")
        return float(pieces[1].split()[0])
    return df.assign(num_bedrm=df["Description"].apply(get_bedrm))

def add_num_bath(df):
    """Adds num_bath column by parsing the Description text."""
    def get_bath(desc):
        details = desc.split("It has a total of ")[1]
        pieces = details.split(", ")
        return float(pieces[2].split()[1])
    return df.assign(num_bath=df["Description"].apply(get_bath))

def id_expensive(df):
    """Adds in_expensive: 1.0 if neighborhood is in top 10 by median sale price."""
    median_by_nbhd = df.groupby("Neighborhood Code")["Sale Price"].median()
    top10 = list(median_by_nbhd.nlargest(10).index)
    return df.assign(in_expensive=np.where(
        df["Neighborhood Code"].isin(top10), 1.0, 0.0
    ))

def expand_wall_material(df):
    """Creates Wall Material Cat dummies (Masonry is reference category)."""
    wall_map = {1: "Wood", 2: "Masonry", 3: "Wood&Masonry", 4: "Stucco"}
    df = df.assign(**{"Wall Material Cat": df["Wall Material"].map(wall_map)})
    for cat in ["Stucco", "Wood", "Wood&Masonry"]:
        col = f"Wall Material Cat_{cat}"
        df = df.assign(**{col: (df["Wall Material Cat"] == cat).astype(int)})
    return df

def add_log_land(df):
    """Adds Log Land Square Feet (clipping at 1 to avoid log(0))."""
    return df.assign(**{
        "Log Land Square Feet": np.log(df["Land Square Feet"].clip(lower=1))
    })

def add_log_estimates(df):
    """Adds log of the assessor's prior-year building and land estimates."""
    return df.assign(**{
        "Log Estimate (Building)": np.log(df["Estimate (Building)"].clip(lower=1)),
        "Log Estimate (Land)":     np.log(df["Estimate (Land)"].clip(lower=1))
    })

def add_central_air_ind(df):
    """Adds is_central_air: 1 if Central Air == 1 (yes), 0 otherwise."""
    return df.assign(is_central_air=(df["Central Air"] == 1).astype(int))

def add_age_features(df):
    """Adds Age squared to capture non-linear age/price relationship."""
    return df.assign(age_sq=df["Age"] ** 2)

def add_quality_features(df):
    """Adds binary quality/design indicators."""
    return df.assign(
        is_good_repair       =(df["Repair Condition"] == 1).astype(int),
        is_architect_design  =(df["Design Plan"]       == 1).astype(int),
        has_cathedral_ceiling=(df["Cathedral Ceiling"] == 1).astype(int)
    )

def add_basement_features(df):
    """Adds has_full_basement: 1 if Basement == 1 (Full)."""
    return df.assign(has_full_basement=(df["Basement"] == 1).astype(int))


def train_and_predict(train_df, test_df):
    """The full pipeline. Trains a multi-variable OLS regression on
    engineered features and returns predictions for the test set."""
    train_filtered = filter_training_data(train_df)

    def engineer(df):
        return (df
                .pipe(log_transforms)
                .pipe(add_intercept)
                .pipe(add_bedrm)
                .pipe(add_num_bath)
                .pipe(id_expensive)
                .pipe(expand_wall_material)
                .pipe(add_log_land)
                .pipe(add_log_estimates)
                .pipe(add_central_air_ind)
                .pipe(add_age_features)
                .pipe(add_quality_features)
                .pipe(add_basement_features))

    train_df = engineer(train_filtered)
    test_df  = engineer(test_df)

    varlist = [
        "intercept",
        "Log Building Square Feet",
        "Log Land Square Feet",
        "Log Estimate (Building)",
        "Log Estimate (Land)",
        "num_bedrm",
        "num_bath",
        "Age",
        "age_sq",
        "Fireplaces",
        "in_expensive",
        "Wall Material Cat_Stucco",
        "Wall Material Cat_Wood",
        "Wall Material Cat_Wood&Masonry",
        "is_central_air",
        "Garage Indicator",
        "is_good_repair",
        "is_architect_design",
        "has_cathedral_ceiling",
        "has_full_basement",
    ]

    X_train = select_vars(train_df, varlist)
    X_test  = select_vars(test_df,  varlist)
    y_train = train_df["Log Sale Price"]
    model   = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train).fit()
    return model.predict(X_test)

Question 15 Summary¶

Features Considered¶

I explored quantitative and categorical variables to build a predictive model for Log Sale Price:

Quantitative Features:

  • Log Building Square Feet – The primary structural size predictor; log transformation linearizes the relationship with price
  • Log Land Square Feet – Lot size drives property value independently of the building itself
  • Log Estimate (Building) – Assessor's prior-year building appraisal; emerged as the strongest new predictor
  • Log Estimate (Land) – Assessor's prior-year land appraisal
  • num_bedrm – Parsed from the Description field; shows negative coefficient when controlling for square footage (smaller rooms signal lower quality)
  • num_bath – Parsed from Description; positive predictor of sale price
  • Age – Newer homes generally command higher prices
  • age_sq – Squared age term captures non-linearity in the age/price relationship
  • Fireplaces – Positive association with price; counts amenity value

Categorical & Binary Features:

  • in_expensive – Binary indicator (1 if property is in top-10 neighborhoods by median sale price)
  • Wall Material dummies – Three binary indicators (Stucco, Wood, Wood&Masonry); Masonry is the reference category
  • is_central_air – Binary (1 if Central Air present)
  • Garage Indicator – Binary (1 if garage present)
  • is_good_repair – Binary (1 if Repair Condition = Above average)
  • is_architect_design – Binary (1 if Design Plan = Architect vs. stock plan)
  • has_cathedral_ceiling – Binary (1 if cathedral ceiling present)
  • has_full_basement – Binary (1 if full basement)

Models Fit and Results¶

I iteratively built and tested multiple models, starting simple and adding complexity:

  • Baseline Model: Intercept + Log Building Square Feet → Local Test MSE ≈ 0.652
  • Question 13a Pipeline: Added num_bedrm, in_expensive, and wall-material dummies → Local Test MSE ≈ 0.620
  • Expanded Quantitative Model: Incorporated Log Land Square Feet, Age, age_sq, and Fireplaces → Progressive MSE reduction
  • Amenity Indicators: Added is_central_air and Garage Indicator → Further improvement
  • Assessor Appraisals Added: Included Log Estimate (Building) and Log Estimate (Land) → Substantial MSE reduction (these appraisals are highly predictive)
  • Full Final Model (Question 15): Added num_bath, quality/design indicators (is_good_repair, is_architect_design, has_cathedral_ceiling), and has_full_basement → Best local test performance

Feature Engineering Approach¶

  • Log transforms applied to Building Sq Ft, Land Sq Ft, and both assessor Estimate columns to reduce right skew and linearize relationships
  • Age + age_sq polynomial captures the U-shaped age/price curve (very new homes and renovated older homes both command premiums)
  • Pure Market Filter restricted training data to arms-length sales only, removing foreclosures and family transfers that introduce noise
  • Building size filter limited observations to 200–15,000 sq ft to exclude implausible entries
  • Consistent dummy variables created manually (rather than via pd.get_dummies) to ensure train and test sets always produce identical columns, even when a category is absent in one set
